title: The Four Operators and 1,388 Lost Minutes: A Manufacturing Downtime Story
description: Analyzing manufacturing line downtime across products, operators, and downtime factors to find where production time really goes.
content:
# The Four Operators and 1,388 Lost Minutes: A Manufacturing Downtime Story

## 1. Opening the logbook

Every factory has one: the downtime logbook. The one nobody likes, but everybody fills. Every time the line stops -- an emergency stop, a jammed conveyor, a spilled batch -- someone writes it down.

In this story, the logbook belongs to a beverage bottling line. It covers 38 batches over five production days, and it records exactly where 1,388 minutes of production time went. That is 23 hours of a line standing still.

The question I wanted to answer was simple: who and what ate those 1,388 minutes? Because if you can answer that, you know where training, maintenance, and inventory fixes will pay off first.

## 2. The data behind the story

The dataset comes from a manufacturing line productivity workbook with four sheets:

| Sheet | Rows | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Line productivity | 38 | One row per batch: date, product, batch ID, operator, start/end time |
| Products | 6 | Product catalog: flavor, size, minimum batch time |
| Downtime factors | 12 | Factor catalog: description + whether it is an operator error |
| Line downtime | 35 | Downtime minutes per batch across 12 factor columns |

### The dirty secret of the downtime sheet

The `Line downtime` sheet looks innocent until you open it. Row 1 is a label row, row 2 is the real header (`Batch`, then factor IDs `1`..`12`), and each subsequent row has minutes scattered across factor columns. When pandas reads it, you get `Unnamed` columns everywhere.

The fix is a two-line reshape:

```python
dt = dt_raw.iloc[2:].copy()
dt.columns = ["Batch"] + [f"F{i}" for i in range(1, 13)]
```

Twelve factor columns map to descriptions through the `Downtime factors` sheet -- and six of them are marked as operator error: batch change, product spill, machine adjustment, batch coding error, calibration error, and label switch.

### Column dictionary

**Line productivity**: Date (batch date), Product (product ID), Batch (unique batch ID), Operator (line operator), Start/End Time (production window).

**Products**: Product (ID), Flavor (orange/lemon-lime/cola/root beer/diet cola), Size (600 ml or 2 L), Min batch time (minutes with no downtime).

**Downtime factors**: Factor (ID 1-12), Description, Operator Error (Yes/No).

**Line downtime**: Batch (FK), then 12 columns of downtime minutes per factor.

## 3. The goal

Management wanted three facts:

1. Which products and batches were hit by downtime?
2. Which operator caused the most errors?
3. Which operator accumulated the longest total downtime?

## 4. How I worked through it

**Step 1 - Reshape downtime.** Read the downtime sheet with `header=None`, take rows from index 2, and assign factor columns manually.

**Step 2 - Compute total downtime per batch.** Each batch's total is the row sum across all 12 factor columns:

```python
dt["total_downtime_min"] = dt.iloc[:, 1:].sum(axis=1)
```

**Step 3 - Join the story together.** Merge operator and product onto each batch via the `Line productivity` sheet, then attach product details from `Products`.

**Step 4 - Split operator error vs everything else.** Sum the six operator-error factor columns separately, so every operator's downtime has two components: their errors and process/machine noise.

**Step 5 - Daily view.** Group downtime by date to see how the week unfolded.

## 5. Finding 1: Every product bleeds, but Cola bleeds most

All six products lost production time across 35 of 38 batches. The damage is not spread evenly:

| Product | Flavor | Batches hit | Total downtime | Avg per batch |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| CO-600 | Cola | 14 | 494 min | 35 min |
| CO-2L | Cola (2L) | 5 | 277 min | 55 min |
| RB-600 | Root beer | 7 | 258 min | 37 min |
| LE-600 | Lemon-lime | 5 | 169 min | 34 min |
| DC-600 | Diet cola | 3 | 115 min | 38 min |
| OR-600 | Orange | 1 | 75 min | 75 min |

The Cola line (CO-600) eats 494 minutes across 14 batches -- one third of all downtime. But look at the two extremes: CO-2L loses 55 minutes per batch on average, and the single OR-600 batch lost 75 minutes. Small-batch products are paying a hefty per-batch price, which makes sense: a 2-liter format is heavier and slower to change over, and the orange batch likely hit a changeover from a different setup.

![Downtime by product](/images/manufacturing/downtime_by_product.png)

## 6. Finding 2: The factor breakdown -- machines and people share the blame

Ranking the 12 factors by total minutes tells a clear story:

| Factor | Operator error? | Minutes | Share | Batches |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Machine adjustment | Yes | 332 | 23.9% | 12 |
| Machine failure | No | 254 | 18.3% | 11 |
| Inventory shortage | No | 225 | 16.2% | 9 |
| Batch change | Yes | 160 | 11.5% | 5 |
| Batch coding error | Yes | 145 | 10.4% | 6 |
| Other | No | 74 | 5.3% | 6 |
| Product spill | Yes | 57 | 4.1% | 3 |
| Calibration error | Yes | 49 | 3.5% | 3 |
| Labeling error | No | 42 | 3.0% | 2 |
| Label switch | Yes | 33 | 2.4% | 3 |
| Conveyor belt jam | No | 17 | 1.2% | 1 |

![Downtime by factor](/images/manufacturing/downtime_by_factor.png)

The headline number: **55.9% of all downtime (776 minutes) is attributed to operator-error factors**. The single biggest factor, machine adjustment (332 min), is operator-classified. That is not a machine problem wearing a human name -- it is a setup/calibration problem that operators own.

The non-operator side is concentrated too: machine failure (254 min) plus inventory shortage (225 min) together account for another third. So the fix list is short: adjust the adjustment procedure, harden the failure-prone machine, and keep more inventory on hand.

## 7. Finding 3: Meet the operators -- Charlie is the story

Four operators ran the line: Charlie, Dee, Dennis, and Mac. Here is the ledger:

| Operator | Total downtime | Share of all | Operator-error minutes | Error share of own time |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Charlie | 384 min | 27.7% | 228 min | 59% |
| Dee | 370 min | 26.7% | 192 min | 52% |
| Mac | 332 min | 23.9% | 192 min | 58% |
| Dennis | 302 min | 21.8% | 164 min | 54% |

![Downtime by operator](/images/manufacturing/downtime_by_operator.png)

Charlie leads on both counts: the longest total downtime (384 minutes) and the most operator-error minutes (228 minutes, 59% of his own total). Dee is right behind him at 370 total / 192 error.

One nuance: Mac has the highest minutes per batch (41.5) because he ran fewer batches (8) than Charlie and Dee (11 each). Per shift, Mac's line stops were the most costly.

And a pattern worth naming: every operator's downtime is majority operator-error -- the lowest share is Dee at 52%. This is not a one-bad-apple story; it is a whole-team operational standard that needs raising (or a standard procedure that needs fixing).

## 8. Finding 4: The week's shape -- Monday was brutal

![Downtime by date](/images/manufacturing/downtime_by_date.png)

| Date | Day | Batches | Downtime | Per batch |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2024-09-02 | Monday | 11 | 503 min | 45.7 min |
| 2024-08-30 | Friday | 12 | 444 min | 37.0 min |
| 2024-08-29 | Thursday | 7 | 244 min | 34.9 min |
| 2024-08-31 | Saturday | 7 | 165 min | 23.6 min |
| 2024-09-03 | Tuesday | 1 | 32 min | 32.0 min |

Monday, September 2, stands out: 503 minutes lost across 11 batches -- 45.7 minutes per batch, the worst ratio of the week. Friday (444 min) is the second-highest. Both days ran the heaviest production load. Saturday was the calmest at 23.6 minutes per batch, which hints that downtime scales with workload -- possibly via rushed changeovers when the day is packed.

The operator-by-date matrix adds color: on Monday, Charlie (191), Dee (163), and Dennis (149) all had heavy losses; Mac was off. Friday's 444 minutes were split among Charlie, Dee, and Dennis again. Highest workload days coincide with the highest-error operators.

## 9. Recommendations

1. **Retrain or re-procedure Charlie first.** He owns 27.7% of all downtime and 59% of his time is operator error. A focused machine-adjustment and batch-change protocol could reclaim most of it.
2. **Fix machine adjustment (332 min) as a process, not a blame.** It is the single largest factor and it is operator-classified -- meaning the standard operating procedure for adjustment is the real culprit. A documented setup checklist is cheap.
3. **Put 254 minutes of machine failure on the maintenance calendar.** One third of non-operator downtime comes from this factor alone.
4. **Review inventory policy for the 225-minute shortage.** Shortages are usually a planning fix, not a floor fix.
5. **Even the load between operators.** Mac averages 41.5 minutes of downtime per batch vs Dee's 33.6. If batch allocation can be balanced, the line loses less.
6. **Treat Monday/Friday rush as a risk flag.** Heavier production days show the worst per-batch downtime; consider pre-shift changeover prep on those days.

## 10. Limitations

1. **Small sample.** 38 batches over 5 days is a short window. Operator rankings could shift with more shifts.
2. **Correlation, not causation.** High downtime days have more batches, but we cannot prove workload caused the extra minutes without shift-level context.
3. **Factor classification is as given.** The dataset marks six factors as operator error; real root-cause would need shift notes or video.
4. **No cost data.** Downtime minutes are counted, but product margins, overtime, and lost sales are not in the workbook -- a minute on OR-600 may cost more than a minute on CO-600.
5. **"Other" factor (74 min) is a black box** -- 5.3% of all downtime is unexplained by the dictionary.

title: Cafe Rewards: Conversion Funnel & Retention Cohort Analysis
description: End-to-end EDA of Cafe Rewards offers, transactions, and customer cohorts -- conversion funnel analysis, unaware completion detection, and retention cohort breakdown.
content:
## 1. Introduction

One of the recurring tasks of a data analyst in retail and F&B is evaluating whether a rewards program actually works: are offers being completed, are rewards being paid to the right people, and is budget producing incremental behavior or subsidizing purchases customers would have made anyway?

This analysis evaluates 10 offers sent by a cafe loyalty program to 17,000 members over a 30-day period.

---

## 2. Dataset Description

Three tables from the Cafe Rewards dataset, documented in `data_dictionary.csv`.

### Tables

`**offers.csv**` -- Catalog of 10 offers. Each has a unique ID, type (bogo, discount, informational), difficulty (minimum spend required, in dollars), reward (amount earned on completion), duration (days to complete), and marketing channels used.

`**customers.csv**` -- Demographic data for 17,000 members: customer ID, join date, gender, age, and estimated annual income.

`**events.csv**` -- 306,534 activity records. Each links a customer to an offer or transaction with a timestamp (hours since start of the 30-day period) and a `value` payload.

### Database figure


| Table | Rows | Cols |
| --------------- | ------- | ---- |
| `offers.csv` | 10 | 6 |
| `customers.csv` | 17,000 | 5 |
| `events.csv` | 306,534 | 4 |


### Offer catalog


| offer_id (prefix) | type | difficulty $ | reward $ | duration days | channels |
| ----------------- | ------------- | ------------ | -------- | ------------- | -------------------------- |
| ae264e... | bogo | 10 | 10 | 7 | email, mobile, social |
| 4d5c57... | bogo | 10 | 10 | 5 | web, email, mobile, social |
| 9b98b8... | bogo | 5 | 5 | 7 | web, email, mobile |
| f19421... | bogo | 5 | 5 | 5 | web, email, mobile, social |
| 0b1e15... | discount | 20 | 5 | 10 | web, email |
| 2298d6... | discount | 7 | 3 | 7 | web, email, mobile, social |
| fafdcd... | discount | 10 | 2 | 10 | web, email, mobile, social |
| 2906b8... | discount | 10 | 2 | 7 | web, email, mobile |
| 3f207d... | informational | 0 | 0 | 4 | web, email, mobile |
| 5a8bc6... | informational | 0 | 0 | 3 | email, mobile, social |


---

## 3. Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Issues

### Data issue 1: Inconsistent JSON keys in `events.value`

The `value` column stores a stringified dict whose key names vary by event type:


| event | key(s) |
| -------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| `offer received`, `offer viewed` | `"offer id"` (space) |
| `offer completed` | `"offer_id"` (underscore) + `"reward"` |
| `transaction` | `"amount"` |


Fix: one `extract()` helper that probes both spellings:

```python
def extract(d, *keys):
    for k in keys:
        if k in d:
            return d[k]
    return None

events["offer_id"] = events["v"].apply(lambda d: extract(d, "offer_id", "offer id"))
events["amount"]   = events["v"].apply(lambda d: extract(d, "amount"))
events["reward_c"] = events["v"].apply(lambda d: extract(d, "reward"))
```

### Data issue 2: A 2,175-row masked block in `customers.csv`

Exactly 2,175 of 17,000 rows (12.8%) have `age=118`, `gender=NaN`, `income=NaN`. Age 118 is impossible (real range 18-101) -- it is a deliberate missing-marker, not a real value. All 2,175 rows are masked together.

**Decision:** These members have real transactions and offer events, so I keep them in funnel, transaction, and tenure analyses but **exclude them from demographic segmentation**, reporting them as a separate "unknown" segment.

### Customer demographics (masked block excluded)



![](/images/cafe-rewards/customer_demographic_distribution.png)


| Variable | Summary |
| ---------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| gender | 8,484 M / 6,129 F / 212 O / 2,175 masked |
| age (clean) | mean 46.2, median 47, range 18-101 |
| income | mean $65,406, median $64,000, $6,700-$120,000 |
| became_member_on | 2013-07-29 -> 2018-07-26 |


---

## 4. Goal of Analysis

### Problem

Optimize offer design and targeting to maximize completion and net value while minimizing reward budget spent on customers who would have purchased anyway.

### Questions

1. How does the conversion funnel compare across offer types, and what explains the differences?
2. How many completion rewards are paid to customers who never viewed the offer?
3. Does transaction behavior relate to offer completion?
4. Which demographic segments convert most effectively?
5. Does membership tenure relate to engagement?
6. Which offers generate the best net value per completion?

---

## 5. Process -- Step by Step

**Step 1 -- Parse and merge.** Parse `events.value` as dict; consolidate `offer_id` keys; dropna on offer_id before offer-level analysis (transaction events lack offer_id by design).

**Step 2 -- Per-offer funnel.** Unique customer counts per stage per offer:

```python
funnel = ev.pivot_table(
    index="offer_id", columns="event", values="customer_id",
    aggfunc="nunique"
).fillna(0).astype(int)
```

**Step 3 -- Unaware completions.** For each `offer completed` event, check whether the customer had an `offer viewed` event for the same offer_id. Completions with no prior view are flagged `unaware`.

**Step 4 -- Reward accounting.** Total rewards paid per offer = sum of `reward` field in `offer completed` events x per-completion reward from offers table. Cost per completion = total rewards / unique completers.

**Step 5 -- Transactions.** Per-customer transaction count and amount during the offer window; correlate with completion rate.

**Step 6 -- Tenure cohort.** Group members by `became_member_on` year; classify active = >=1 transaction in 30 days.

**Step 7 -- Demographic segmentation.** Income quartiles x gender x offer type, masked block reported separately.

---

## 6. Findings

### 6.1 Conversion funnel -- all 10 offers

![](/images/cafe-rewards/funnel_per_offer.png)




| offer_id (prefix) | type | diff | reward $ | dur | received | viewed | completed | view % | complete % |
| ----------------- | ------------- | ---- | -------- | --- | -------- | ------ | --------- | ------ | ---------- |
| ae264e... | bogo | 10 | 10 | 7 | 6,374 | 5,696 | 3,177 | 89.4 | 49.8 |
| 4d5c57... | bogo | 10 | 10 | 5 | 6,330 | 6,132 | 2,885 | 96.9 | 45.6 |
| 9b98b8... | bogo | 5 | 5 | 7 | 6,355 | 3,658 | 3,784 | 57.6 | 59.5 |
| f19421... | bogo | 5 | 5 | 5 | 6,262 | 6,060 | 3,741 | 96.8 | 59.7 |
| 0b1e15... | discount | 20 | 5 | 10 | 6,374 | 2,400 | 2,978 | 37.7 | 46.7 |
| 2298d6... | discount | 7 | 3 | 7 | 6,325 | 6,122 | 4,421 | 96.8 | 69.9 |
| fafdcd... | discount | 10 | 2 | 10 | 6,332 | 6,150 | 4,530 | 97.1 | 71.5 |
| 2906b8... | discount | 10 | 2 | 7 | 6,285 | 3,608 | 3,480 | 57.4 | 55.4 |
| 3f207d... | informational | 0 | 0 | 4 | 6,331 | 3,635 | 0 | 57.4 | 0 |
| 5a8bc6... | informational | 0 | 0 | 3 | 6,320 | 5,674 | 0 | 89.8 | 0 |


**Aggregate:** 16,994 members received >=1 offer; 12,774 (75.2%) completed >=1. Total rewards paid: 164,676. Average reward per completion: 4.90.

**Key funnel findings:**

- View rate is a **channel-coverage problem**, not offer quality. Offers on all 4 channels reach ~97% view rate; `0b1e15` (web + email only) is 37.7%.
- Discounts complete more often than BOGOs at lower cost: 71.5% (discount, $2 reward) vs 49.8% (bogo, $10 reward).
- Informational offers view 57-90% but complete 0% by design.
- 

### 6.2 Difficulty, type, and duration interaction

![](/images/cafe-rewards/difficulty_sensitivity_curve.png)

Difficulty alone is misleading. The interaction with type and duration matters:

- Difficulty 7-10 with discount type and 7-10 day duration -> 55-72% completion
- Difficulty 10 with BOGO and 5-7 day duration -> 46-50% completion
- Difficulty 20 -> cliff to 47% regardless of type

The sweet spot is **difficulty 7-10 + discount + 7-10 day duration**.



### 6.3 Unaware completions: paying for behavior that already happened

![](/images/cafe-rewards/unaware_completion_per_offer.png)



A completion event means the customer spent enough during the window -- but did they actually *see* the offer? 15.6% of completions happened with no prior `offer viewed` event.


| Offer type | Unaware completions | % of completions |
| ---------- | ------------------- | ---------------- |
| Discount | 2,744 | 12.1% |
| BOGO | 2,062 | 10.7% |
| **Total** | **4,536** | **15.6%** |


Offer `0b1e15` (discount, difficulty 20) is the worst offender: 51% of its completions are from customers who never viewed it. This is the clearest sign of **wasted reward budget** -- paying rewards for purchases that happened organically.

### 6.4 Transaction behavior vs completion

![](/images/cafe-rewards/transaction_amount_vs_completion.png)




| Statistic | Value |
| ------------------------------------- | -------- |
| Mean transaction | 12.78 |
| Median transaction | 8.89 |
| Max transaction | 1,062.28 |
| Transactions <= 7.70 (avg difficulty) | 46.7% |


- Customers who complete offers transact more frequently: mean 9.3 transactions vs 5.5 for non-completers.
- Average transaction amount doesn't strongly predict individual completion (per-transaction r ~ 0.13).
- **Frequency, not magnitude** is the stronger behavioral signal -- consistent with offers rewarding repeat visitors.
- 

### 6.5 Cost efficiency: completion rate vs reward cost

![](/images/cafe-rewards/cost_per_completion.png)




| Offer type | Difficulty | Reward | Completion rate | Cost per completion |
| ----------- | ---------- | ------ | --------------- | ------------------- |
| Discount $2 | 10 | 2 | 71.5% | 0.74 |
| Discount $3 | 7 | 3 | 69.9% | 0.88 |
| Discount $5 | 20 | 5 | 46.7% | 5.70 |
| BOGO $5 | 5 | 5 | 59.5% | 5.79 |
| BOGO $10 | 10 | 10 | 45.6-49.8% | 11.50 |


Discount offers at 2-3 reward are 7-15x more cost-efficient per completion than 10 BOGOs, even when completion rates are similar.

### 6.6 Demographic segments (masked 2,175 excluded)

![](/images/cafe-rewards/income_quartile_completion.png)



#### By income quartile


| Income quartile | BOGO complete | Discount complete |
| ---------------- | ------------- | ----------------- |
| <25th percentile | 41% | 52% |
| 25-50th | 56% | 64% |
| 50-75th | 66% | 71% |
| >=75th | 77% | 81% |


Completion rises monotonically with income -- the gap is 36pp for BOGO, 29pp for discount.

#### Gender within income (disentangled)

When we hold income constant, the gender gap shrinks but persists:


| Gender | Income <25th | Income >=75th |
| ------ | ------------ | ------------- |
| Female | 55% | **78%** |
| Male | 35% | **67%** |
| Other | 51% | **75%** |


The ~5-10pp gender gap is **partly driven by income** (women have higher median income in this dataset), but a residual gap (~5pp) remains even within income bands, suggesting a genuine behavioral difference.

#### Unknown demographics segment

2,175 members (12.8%) have masked age/gender/income. Their completion rate is 12-21% -- dramatically lower than any known segment. They consume offers at the same rate but convert poorly.



### 6.7 Retention cohort (by join year)

![](/images/cafe-rewards/cohort_retention_curve.png)




| Join year | Active rate | Completion rate |
| ------------------ | ----------- | --------------- |
| 2017-2018 (newest) | 68% | 55% |
| 2015-2016 (mid) | 45% | 42% <- trough |
| 2013-2014 (oldest) | 65% | 48% |


- Newest members are most engaged (onboarding effect).
- The **2015-2016 cohort underperforms** both adjacent cohorts by ~20pp on activity -- a retention leak worth investigating.
- This is cross-sectional (one 30-day window); it cannot show retention decay over time.

---

## 7. Recommendations

1. **Send every offer on all four channels.** `0b1e15` (discount, difficulty 20) is viewed by only 37.7% -- adding missing channels is a free completion boost.
2. **Route by income segment.** Top-quartile income customers complete 77-81%; bottom quartile completes 41-52%. Use low-difficulty discounts for lower-income segments.
3. **Target high-frequency transactors.** Customers with >=4 transactions during offer window complete 19pp more often. Micro-spenders can be re-targeted with lower-difficulty offers.
4. **Deprioritize 10 BOGOs.** They cost 11.50 per completion against 0.74-0.88 for 2-3 discounts. Keep only if basket-size lift justifies the 15x cost premium.
5. **Suppress reward offers for unaware-prone customers.** 15.6% of completions go to customers who never viewed the offer -- implement a spend-threshold filter (if customer spent >= difficulty organically in past 30 days, skip the offer).
6. **Investigate the 2015-2016 cohort.** It lags both older (survivors) and newer (onboarding) cohorts by ~20pp -- likely a data or product issue that warrants root-cause analysis.

---

## 8. Limitations

1. **No causal attribution.** We cannot prove the offer caused the purchase -- only that spending occurred during the window. Net effect is a proxy, not true incremental ROI.
2. **No transaction-offer linkage.** Transaction events do not carry `offer_id`, so we cannot attribute specific transaction amounts to specific offers. Transaction analysis is at the customer level only.
3. **30-day window.** Cannot observe seasonality, repeat campaign effects, or retention decay over time.
4. **Self-selection bias.** Customers who view offers may differ systematically from those who don't.
5. **Income is estimated.** Described as "estimated annual income" -- likely model-imputed, introducing measurement error at the strongest predictor variable.
6. **75% of offers have identical channel sets**, making it hard to isolate channel effects; difficulty, duration, and type are confounded across the 10 offers.
7. **Small sample for gender "O".** The third gender category (n~212-303) is too small for robust conclusions.

title: Finding Transaction Value vs Offer Completion: A Study Case on Coffee Promotion
description: Analyzing how transaction amount, frequency, and timing correlate with offer completion in the Cafe Rewards dataset.
content:
# Finding Transaction Value vs Offer Completion: A Study Case on Coffee Promotion

## 1. EDA — Dataset Description

### Source
Three tables from the Cafe Rewards loyalty program (coffee shop rewards), located at `D:/FREELANCING/Cafe Rewards Offers/`. A data dictionary file (`data_dictionary.csv`) documents each column.

### Database Figure
| Table | Rows | Cols | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| `offers.csv` | 10 | 6 | Offer catalog (look-up table) |
| `customers.csv` | 17,000 | 5 | Member demographics |
| `events.csv` | 306,534 | 4 | Activity log |
| `data_dictionary.csv` | 19 | 3 | Column descriptions |

### What each table is about
- **`offers.csv`**: Catalog of 10 offers with offer type (bogo/discount/informational), difficulty, reward, duration, and channels.
- **`customers.csv`**: Demographic data for 17,000 members (gender, age, income, join date).
- **`events.csv`**: 306,534 activity records — transactions, offer received/viewed/completed. Each has a stringified-dict `value` column.

### Column descriptions

**`events.csv`**
| Column | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| customer_id | string | Member who triggered the event |
| event | string | transaction / offer received / offer viewed / offer completed |
| value | string | Stringified dict — keys vary by event type |
| time | int | Hours since start of 30-day window (0-714) |

### Key data quirk: inconsistent JSON keys in `value`
- `offer received` / `offer viewed` → key `"offer id"` (with space)
- `offer completed` → `"offer_id"` (underscore) + `reward`
- `transaction` → `"amount"` **only** — no offer linkage

This means transactions cannot be directly tied to a specific offer, but we **can** analyze transaction behavior at the **customer level** and compare it to whether that customer ever completes any offer.

### Customer demographics (after masking age=118, which is a deliberate missing-marker)
| Variable | Summary |
|---|---|
| gender | 8,484 M / 6,129 F / 212 O / 2,175 masked |
| age | Mean 46.2, median 47, range 18-101 |
| income | Mean \$65,406, median \$64,000, \$6,700-\$120,000 |
| became_member_on | 2013-07-29 → 2018-07-26 |

---

## 2. Goal of Analysis

### Problem
Cafe Rewards wants to understand whether transaction value (amount, frequency, timing) is predictive of offer completion — and if so, what spending behaviors characterize customers who actually complete offers.

### Questions to answer
1. Do customers who complete offers spend more per transaction?
2. Do they transact more frequently?
3. Is there an hourly pattern — do completions correlate with when people transact?
4. How strong is the overall correlation between spending and completion likelihood?

### Goals
- Quantify spending behavior differences between completion-prone and inactive-completers
- Compute correlation strength for targeting model features
- Surface actionable segments for offer personalization

---

## 3. Process — Step by Step

### Step 1: Identify completion-prone customers
```python
ev = events.dropna(subset=["offer_id"])
cust_completed = set(ev[ev["event"]=="offer completed"]["customer_id"])
```
→ 12,774 customers (75.1%) ever completed ≥1 offer.

### Step 2: Extract all transaction records (no offer linkage possible)
```python
txn_all = events[events["event"]=="transaction"].copy()
txn_all["amount"] = pd.to_numeric(txn_all["amount"])
txn_all["comp_binary"] = txn_all["customer_id"].isin(cust_completed).astype(int)
```

### Step 3: Aggregate per customer
```python
spend = txn_all.groupby(["customer_id","group"])["amount"].sum()
avg_txn = txn_all.groupby(["customer_id","group"])["amount"].mean()
n_txn = txn_all.groupby(["customer_id","group"]).size()
```

### Step 4: Visualise & correlate
Four-panel chart + Pearson correlation via `scipy.stats.pointbiserialr`.

```python
r, p = pointbiserialr(df["comp_binary"], df["amount"])
```

---

## 4. Findings

![Transaction vs completion](transaction_value_vs_completion.png)

### 4.1 Correlations (completion vs spending metrics)

| Metric | Correlation (r) |
|---|---|
| Per-customer total spend | **0.376** |
| Per-customer avg txn amount | 0.313 |
| Per-customer txn count | 0.318 |
| Individual txn amount | 0.126 |

Moderate correlation (r≈0.38) confirms that **cumulative lifetime spending**, not a single large transaction, is the strongest spending-related predictor of offer completion.

### 4.2 Spending gap between segments

| Metric | Completion-prone | No completion | Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| Total spend / customer | \$133.0 (median \$105) | \$20.0 (median \$13) | **5.8×** |
| Avg txn amount | \$16.42 | \$4.48 | **3.7×** |
| # transactions / customer | 9.3 | 5.5 | 1.7× |

Completion-prone customers spend nearly 6× more in total, transact 1.7× more often, and have 3.7× larger average transaction sizes.

### 4.3 Hourly pattern
The hourly P(ever-completed | transaction at hour) chart shows a **baseline around 75%** throughout the 30-day window — no strong U-curve or spike at specific hours. This suggests offer completion is driven more by **who** transacts (a customer-level trait) than by **when** they transact.

---

## 5. Recommendations

1. **Segment by spend tier**: prioritize high-frequency, high-avg-txn customers (>\$10 avg txn) for offer completion — they convert ~5-6× more reliably.
2. **Don't chase big-spenders only**: individual txn size matters (r=0.13) but cumulative spend does more (r=0.38) — a customer with 8 × \$6 txns beats one with 1 × \$48 txn.
3. **Timing is secondary**: since hourly patterns are flat, schedule offers based on channel reachability (email vs push) rather than trying to micro-optimize send time.

---

## 6. Limitations

1. **No transaction-offer linkage**: transaction events do not carry `offer_id`, so we cannot attribute a specific transaction to a specific offer. All analysis is at the **customer level**, not per-offer.
2. **Correlation, not causation**: high spend precedes/matches completion, but does not prove that completing offers causes more spending (or vice versa).
3. **Self-selection bias**: customers who complete offers are inherently more engaged, so spending differences may reflect engagement rather than offer design.
4. **30-day window**: all data is confined to one 30-day period — no seasonality or long-term behavior patterns.
5. **306,534 transactions** span only 17,000 customers (~9 transactions each), so very low-frequency customers are under-represented.

title: Analisis Churn Nasabah Bank: dari Data Kotor ke Model Prediksi
description: Studi kasus data science end-to-end: membersihkan data nasabah yang berantakan dari Excel (duplikat, simbol mata uang, nilai hilang, kolom rusak), mengungkap profil nasabah yang rawan pergi, dan membangun model prediksi churn dengan Python.
content:
Bank kehilangan nasabah setiap bulan. Pertanyaannya bukan hanya "berapa banyak", tapi "siapa" — dan apa yang bisa dilakukan sebelum mereka pergi. Studi kasus ini mengerjakan itu dari nol: mulai dari file Excel yang berantakan, sampai model yang bisa menilai risiko churn tiap nasabah.

## 1. Eksplorasi data awal (EDA)

### Asal data dan gambaran umum

Dataset ini adalah varian publik dari bank customer churn yang umum dipakai untuk latihan prediksi churn (topik: nasabah berhenti menggunakan layanan bank). Data diterima dalam dua bentuk:

- `Bank_Churn_Messy.xlsx` — versi "kotor" yang sengaja dipecah jadi dua sheet, dengan berbagai masalah kualitas data.
- `Bank_Churn.csv` — versi bersih (referensi) berisi 10.000 nasabah × 13 kolom, dipakai sebagai acuan verifikasi.

Struktur database:

```
Bank_Churn_Messy.xlsx
├── Sheet: Customer_Info (10.001 baris — data pribadi)
│     CustomerId · Surname · CreditScore · Geography · Gender · Age · Tenure* · EstimatedSalary
└── Sheet: Account_Info  (10.002 baris — data rekening)
      CustomerId · Balance · NumOfProducts · HasCrCard · Tenure* · IsActiveMember · Exited
      └─ digabung lewat CustomerId (kunci utama nasabah)
Bank_Churn.csv (referensi bersih, 10.000 baris × 13 kolom — untuk QA)
(*) Tenure ada di kedua sheet dan konsisten — dipakai sebagai cross-check saat merge
```

### Data dictionary — deskripsi tiap kolom

| Kolom | Tipe | Deskripsi |
|---|---|---|
| CustomerId | int | ID unik nasabah |
| Surname | str | Nama belakang nasabah |
| CreditScore | int | Skor kredit (rentang ~350-850) |
| Geography | str | Negara: France, Spain, Germany |
| Gender | str | Jenis kelamin: Male / Female |
| Age | int | Usia (18-92 tahun) |
| Tenure | int | Lama menjadi nasabah (tahun, 0-10) |
| Balance | float | Saldo rekening (Euro) |
| NumOfProducts | int | Jumlah produk bank yang digunakan (1-4) |
| HasCrCard | 0/1 | Punya kartu kredit (1 = ya) |
| IsActiveMember | 0/1 | Nasabah aktif (1 = ya) |
| EstimatedSalary | float | Estimasi gaji tahunan (Euro) |
| Exited | 0/1 | **Target**: churn (1 = nasabah pergi) |

### Statistik ringkas

```python
df.describe().T
df.isna().sum()          # 0 missing di versi bersih
df.Exited.value_counts(normalize=True)
# 0 → 79,6%  |  1 → 20,4%
```

- 10.000 nasabah, 13 kolom, tidak ada nilai hilang di versi bersih.
- Churn rate keseluruhan: 20,4% — kelas minoritas tapi cukup besar untuk dipelajari.
- Saldo: 36% nasabah bersaldo 0; median saldo €97rb.
- Umur rata-rata 39 tahun; skor kredit rata-rata 650; tenure rata-rata 5 tahun.
- 70,6% punya kartu kredit; 51,5% nasabah aktif.

## 2. Tujuan analisis

### Problem dataset

- File sumber berantakan: duplikat, simbol mata uang di kolom angka, label negara ganda ("France"/"French"/"FRA"), nilai hilang terselubung (-€999999), dan data pribadi terbelah dari data rekening. Analisis apa pun tidak bisa dimulai sebelum data dibersihkan.
- Pertanyaan bisnis di baliknya: churn nasabah adalah kebocoran pendapatan. Bank perlu tahu nasabah seperti apa yang rawan pergi, dan apakah risiko itu bisa dikenali lebih awal.

### Pertanyaan yang dijawab

1. Seberapa besar masalah churn di dataset ini?
2. Siapa nasabah yang paling mungkin churn — profil demografi dan perilaku apa yang membedakan mereka?
3. Faktor mana yang paling berpengaruh terhadap churn?
4. Seberapa akurat churn bisa diprediksi dari data yang tersedia?

### Goal yang ingin dicapai

1. Menghasilkan dataset bersih yang terverifikasi (bukan sekadar "dibersihkan", tapi terbukti cocok dengan referensi).
2. Menemukan segmen nasabah risiko tinggi yang bisa jadi target program retensi.
3. Membangun model prediksi dengan performa yang diukur jujur (ROC-AUC, F1) — bukan sekadar akurasi.

## 3. Proses langkah demi langkah

### 3.1 Data cleaning

Data awal berbentuk Excel dengan dua sheet terpisah, 10.001 dan 10.002 baris. Alurnya: baca kedua sheet, identifikasi semua jenis masalah, bereskan satu per satu, lalu verifikasi terhadap referensi bersih.

**a) Baca dua sheet dan cek duplikat**

```python
cust = pd.read_excel(SRC, sheet_name="Customer_Info")
acct = pd.read_excel(SRC, sheet_name="Account_Info")
cust.CustomerId.duplicated().sum()   # 1 baris
acct.CustomerId.duplicated().sum()   # 2 baris
```

Duplikatnya ternyata baris yang sama persis (salinan ganda), jadi cukup `drop_duplicates(keep="first")` — aman, tidak ada informasi yang hilang.

**b) Normalisasi kategori dan parse mata uang**

```python
geo_map = {"FRA": "France", "French": "France"}
cust["Geography"] = cust["Geography"].replace(geo_map)

def parse_money(s):
    return pd.to_numeric(s.astype(str).str.replace("€", ""), errors="coerce")

cust["EstimatedSalary"] = parse_money(cust["EstimatedSalary"])
acct["Balance"] = parse_money(acct["Balance"])
```

Kolom "France", "French", "FRA" ternyata merujuk negara yang sama. Simbol euro dibuang, lalu string diubah ke angka.

**c) Temukan nilai hilang terselubung (sentinel)**

```python
SENTINEL = -999999.0
cust.loc[cust["EstimatedSalary"] == SENTINEL, "EstimatedSalary"] = pd.NA
```

Tiga nasabah punya gaji "-€999999" — angka negatif mustahil itu adalah penanda data hilang, bukan nilai asli. Ketiganya juga kehilangan Age dan Surname. Karena 0,03% data dan tidak bisa dipulihkan, barisnya di-drop (didokumentasikan, bukan diam-diam).

**d) Temuan: kolom yang rusak permanen di sumber**

Setelah menggabungkan dua sheet dan membandingkannya dengan referensi, QA menemukan 4.992 baris tidak cocok di kolom "punya kartu kredit". Penelusuran menunjukkan kolom itu di file sumber adalah **salinan persis** kolom "nasabah aktif":

```python
(acct["HasCrCard"] == acct["IsActiveMember"]).mean()   # 1.0 → 100% identik
pd.crosstab(acct["HasCrCard"], ref["IsActiveMember_clean"])
# baris diagonal penuh: HasCrCard_messy = IsActiveMember_clean
```

Artinya nilai asli sudah tertimpa saat file dibuat dan **tidak bisa dipulihkan dari sumber mana pun**. Imputasi statistik akan menciptakan data palsu — jadi kolom ini dikeluarkan dari analisis. Pelajaran penting: data cleaning juga berarti tahu kapan data *tidak bisa* diselamatkan.

**e) Verifikasi hasil (QA wajib)**

```python
same_rows = (df3 == r3).all(axis=1).sum()
# 9997/9997 baris identik di 12 kolom yang dibandingkan — 100%
```

Setiap baris hasil dibandingkan dengan referensi bersih yang diketahui benar. Reproducible: seluruh proses ada di satu script `clean_churn.py`.

### 3.2 Eksplorasi pola churn

Dengan data bersih, hitung churn rate per kelompok. Tanpa visualisasi dulu pun polanya terbaca:

```python
df.groupby("Geography").Exited.mean()
# Germany 0.325 | Spain 0.167 | France 0.162

df["age_bin"] = pd.cut(df.Age, bins=[0,25,35,45,55,65,100],
                       labels=["<25","25-34","35-44","45-54","55-64","65+"])
df.groupby("age_bin", observed=True).Exited.mean()
# 55-64 0.498 | 45-54 0.481 | 35-44 0.177 | 65+ 0.152 | <25 0.088 | 25-34 0.078
```

![Churn rate per fitur utama](/images/churn-eda.png)

Polanya dirangkum di bagian Temuan.

### 3.3 Model prediksi

**a) Pipeline: data mentah → fitur → model**

```python
pre = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", StandardScaler(), NUM),
    ("cat", OneHotEncoder(drop="first", handle_unknown="ignore"), CAT),
], remainder="passthrough")   # penting: kolom biner ikut masuk model
```

Catatan penting yang ditemukan saat mengerjakan: tanpa `remainder="passthrough"`, ColumnTransformer diam-diam membuang kolom yang tidak terdaftar — dua fitur biner tidak pernah masuk model, dan performa melonjak setelah diperbaiki.

**b) Perbandingan tiga model**

Data dibagi 80% latih / 20% uji (stratified agar proporsi churn sama), lalu threshold probabilitas di-tune untuk memaksimalkan F1:

| Model | ROC-AUC | F1 | Recall |
|---|---|---|---|
| Logistic Regression (baseline) | 0,777 | 0,51 | 0,60 |
| HistGradientBoosting | 0,861 | 0,63 | 0,63 |
| **Random Forest (balanced)** | **0,865** | **0,63** | **0,66** |

```python
models = {
    "Logistic Regression": LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000, class_weight="balanced"),
    "Random Forest": RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=500, max_depth=10,
                                            class_weight="balanced"),
    "HistGradientBoosting": HistGradientBoostingClassifier(max_iter=300, learning_rate=0.05),
}
```

`class_weight="balanced"` penting karena kelas churn minoritas (20%). Random Forest menang tipis dan dipilih karena mudah dijelaskan ke bisnis.

![Kurva ROC ketiga model](/images/churn-model-roc.png)

![Feature importance Random Forest](/images/churn-model-importance.png)

### 3.4 Eksplorasi lanjutan: interaksi fitur, SHAP, dan ekonomi model

Analisis satu-variabel dan model dasar sudah selesai. Lapisan berikutnya: apakah efek fitur saling menumpuk (A), bisa tidaknya model dijelaskan per nasabah (B), dan apakah model benar-benar bernilai uang (C).

**a) Interaksi fitur: siapa segmen paling berisiko?**

```python
piv = df.pivot_table(index="Geography", columns="age_bin", values="Exited", aggfunc="mean")
#            <25   25-34   35-44   45-54   55-64    65+
# France   0.059   0.054   0.144   0.416   0.463   0.099
# Germany  0.156   0.129   0.284   0.648   0.663   0.300
# Spain    0.089   0.081   0.135   0.388   0.386   0.113
```

![Interaksi fitur: negara × usia, dan produk × keaktifan](/images/churn-interaction.png)

Penemuan penting dari heatmap: **efek Jerman muncul di semua kelompok umur** (rasio churn Jerman vs Perancis konsisten ~2x di setiap baris). Artinya negara dan usia adalah risiko yang *menumpuk*, bukan saling menggantikan — nasabah Jerman tetap lebih berisiko bahkan di usia 25-34.

Lalu siapa segmen paling bahaya? Bukan yang 3+ produk (jumlahnya sedikit):

```python
seg = (df.groupby(["Geography","age_bin","prod_bin","active_lbl"], observed=True)
         .Exited.agg(["size","mean"]))
seg[seg["size"]>=30].sort_values("mean", ascending=False).head(3)
# Jerman  55-64  1 produk  Tidak aktif   n=50   churn 96%
# Perancis 55-64 1 produk  Tidak aktif   n=66   churn 94%
# Jerman  45-54  1 produk  Tidak aktif   n=176  churn 84%
```

Pola yang paling konsisten justru: **1 produk + tidak aktif + usia 45+ = bom waktu** (84-96% churn). Nasabah 2 produk selalu paling aman di semua kombinasi — "two products" adalah pelindung terkuat, dan 3+ produk berisiko tinggi tapi jarang (n kecil).

**b) SHAP: menjelaskan keputusan model per nasabah**

Random Forest adalah kotak hitam. SHAP (TreeExplainer) menghitung kontribusi tiap fitur terhadap prediksi satu nasabah:

```python
explainer = shap.TreeExplainer(pipe.named_steps["clf"])
sv = explainer.shap_values(Xtr_t)[1]   # kelas churn
```

![SHAP summary plot](/images/churn-shap.png)

Ranking SHAP mengkonfirmasi feature importance (umur > jumlah produk > keaktifan > negara Jerman), tapi dengan nilai tambah: model bisa menjawab "mengapa nasabah ini di-flag" — misalnya *"karena usia 58 (kontribusi +0,18), tidak aktif (+0,07), dan tinggal di Jerman (+0,05)"*. Ini yang membuat model bisa dipakai tim retensi dengan percaya diri, bukan sekadar skor.

**c) Ekonomi model: apakah model bernilai uang?**

Uji yang paling jujur: bandingkan net value model vs kontak acak, dengan asumsi nilai nasabah = estimasi gaji tahunan (yang bisa diselamatkan kalau tidak churn) dan biaya kontak per nasabah:

```python
for t in thrs:
    flagged = proba >= t
    value = test.loc[flagged & (test.y==1), "salary"].sum()
    cost = flagged.sum() * CONTACT_COST
    net = value - cost
# baseline acak: kontak n orang acak -> n * (P(churn)*gaji_rata2 - biaya)
```

![Cost-benefit threshold dan pendapatan berisiko per segmen](/images/churn-economics.png)

Hasilnya mengejutkan dan jujur: **dengan nilai = estimasi gaji, model tidak mengalahkan kontak acak** (gap €-527 ribu di semua biaya kontak). Penyebabnya: EstimatedSalary nyaris tidak berkorelasi dengan churn, jadi "nilai yang diselamatkan" model sama saja dengan acak. Pelajaran penting: model yang akurat secara statistik (AUC 0,865) belum tentu menang secara finansial — ROI bergantung pada asumsi nilai nasabah yang sebenarnya (LTV, margin bank), yang tidak tersedia di dataset ini.

Yang tetap berguna: **dengan kapasitas kontak terbatas** (misal hanya budget untuk 200 nasabah), model mengurutkan risiko jauh lebih baik dari acak — itulah fungsi utamanya sebagai alat prioritisasi. Dan peta pendapatan berisiko (gaji churner per segmen) menunjukkan Jerman 45-54 (€29,7 juta) dan Perancis 35-54 (€57,9 juta gabungan) sebagai area nilai terbesar.

## 4. Temuan

### Profil nasabah risiko tinggi

- **Negara**: Jerman 32,5%, jauh di atas Perancis 16,2% dan Spanyol 16,7% — hampir 2x lipat. Efek Jerman konsisten di semua kelompok umur (risiko menumpuk, bukan saling menggantikan).
- **Usia**: churn naik tajam setelah 35, memuncak di 45-64 (~50%), lalu turun di 65+. Usia 25-34 justru paling aman (7,8%).
- **Jumlah produk**: kurva U terbalik. Nasabah dengan 2 produk paling setia (7,6%); 3 produk 82,7%; 4 produk 100%. Nasabah yang "over-bundled" justru kabur. Di semua kombinasi, 2 produk selalu paling aman.
- **Interaksi (temuan baru)**: segmen paling berbahaya justru *1 produk + tidak aktif + usia 45+* (84-96% churn) — bukan yang 3+ produk (n kecil).
- **Keaktifan**: nasabah tidak aktif churn hampir 2x nasabah aktif (26,9% vs 14,3%).
- **Jenis kelamin**: perempuan 25,1% vs laki-laki 16,5%.
- **Saldo**: saldo 0 paling aman (13,9%); saldo >200k churn 55,9% — tapi ini kelompok kecil (34 orang), jadi tidak dipaksakan jadi kesimpulan.
- **Skor kredit**: <400 = 100% churn (19 orang, n kecil); di atas 500 relatif rata ~20%.
- **Tenure**: hampir tidak berpengaruh — flat 17-23% di semua tingkat.

Gambaran besarnya: nasabah paling setia itu muda (<35), pakai 2 produk, dan aktif. Nasabah Jerman usia 45-60 dengan 3+ produk adalah segmen risiko tinggi — tapi yang benar-benar "bom waktu" (84-96%) adalah nasabah 1 produk, tidak aktif, usia 45+.

### Performa model

- Random Forest (balanced): ROC-AUC 0,865, F1 0,63 — dengan threshold 0,56 model menangkap 66% nasabah yang benar-benar churn (recall), dan 61% prediksinya tepat sasaran (precision).
- Fitur terkuat (SHAP mengkonfirmasi): umur, jumlah produk, status keaktifan, dan negara Jerman. SHAP memungkinkan menjelaskan keputusan per nasabah ("kenapa di-flag") — krusial untuk dipakai tim bisnis.
- **Ekonomi (temuan kunci)**: model akurat secara statistik TAPI tidak mengalahkan kontak acak secara finansial ketika nilai nasabah = estimasi gaji (gap €-527 ribu). EstimatedSalary nyaris tidak berkorelasi dengan churn. Nilai model yang sebenarnya: **prioritisasi** — mengurutkan siapa yang paling berisiko untuk kapasitas kontak terbatas, dan memetakan pendapatan berisiko per segmen (Jerman 45-54 = €29,7 juta; Perancis 35-54 = €57,9 juta gabungan).

### Satu kalimat untuk bisnis

*Nasabah yang paling mungkin pergi bisa dikenali dari data demografi dan perilaku produk — sebelum mereka benar-benar pergi.* Rekomendasi turunannya: program retensi khusus untuk segmen risiko tinggi (Jerman, usia 45+, 3+ produk, tidak aktif — dan terutama 1 produk + tidak aktif + usia 45+), dan evaluasi ulang bundling produk yang ternyata justru mengusir nasabah.

## 5. Keterbatasan

- **Tidak ada data transaksi atau riwayat interaksi** — fitur yang biasanya paling prediktif untuk churn tidak tersedia.
- **Threshold model di-tune pada set uji**, jadi angka performa sedikit optimistis terhadap data baru.
- **Satu kolom (HasCrCard) rusak permanen di sumber** dan tidak bisa dipakai — model kehilangan satu fitur yang berpotensi relevan.
- **Analisis ekonomi masih asumsi sederhana**: nilai nasabah diproksikan dengan estimasi gaji (padahal LTV/margin bank yang sebenarnya tidak diketahui), dan biaya kontak diasumsikan flat. Di data nyata, analisis ROI butuh data biaya retensi & nilai nasabah aktual.
- Dataset ini **varian publik untuk latihan** — distribusi dan perilaku nasabah bank sungguhan bisa berbeda, jadi hasilnya butuh validasi ulang sebelum dipakai di produksi.
- Hasil bagus untuk mengurutkan risiko, **bukan** untuk keputusan otomatis per nasabah tanpa validasi lapangan.

Perangkat: Python (pandas, scikit-learn, matplotlib, shap). Seluruh pipeline — dari Excel kotor ke model — dapat dijalankan ulang dari tiga script.

title: Fixing 10,000 Messy Product Names with a Google Sheets Add-on I Built for Free
description: I built a simple Google Sheets extension to help doing redundant tasks, with help of Mistral AI.
